text: All three classifiers are implemented with scikit-learn.
Random forests combine tree predictors, each grown on an independently sampled random vector.
Gradient boosting fits an additive expansion of regression trees by stagewise steepest descent on a loss, including the multiclass logistic likelihood for classification.
Label noise can lower prediction accuracy and raise both model complexity and the number of training samples needed.
With 5% of training labels flipped at random, AdaBoost's test error rose markedly on most of nine datasets, while random forests generally changed little.
With 20% random class noise, bagged C4.5 beat AdaBoost C4.5 on 6 of 9 domains and lost on none, reversing AdaBoost's advantage at 0% noise.

text: For any convex potential booster (including AdaBoost and LogitBoost) and any nonzero random-classification-noise rate, there is a data set that the booster learns without noise but cannot learn to accuracy better than 1/2 with noise, even with early stopping or an L1 bound.
Risk minimization under 0-1 loss is tolerant to label noise, under squared loss it is tolerant only to uniform noise, and under other losses it is not noise tolerant.
None of the standard convex losses satisfies a sufficient condition for risk minimization to be tolerant to uniform label noise, whereas the 0-1, sigmoid, ramp and probit losses do.
A convex, negatively unbounded 'unhinged' loss is robust to symmetric label noise, and strong l2 regularisation makes most standard learners robust to symmetric label noise.

Under class-conditional random label noise, surrogate losses can be corrected (by an unbiased estimator or a weighting), so that methods such as weighted logistic regression are provably noise tolerant.
An injection study on five class-imbalanced software-engineering datasets recommended random forests for building classifiers from noisy data.

In a benchmark of 14 binary tabular datasets with labels flipped completely at random, random forests did very well without noise but became among the worst methods once noise was added, while logistic regression and linear SVC were only slightly sensitive to label corruption.

In a study of XGBoost alone (no random forest or other model family was compared), gradient-boosted decision trees were found to be naturally robust to label noise, particularly symmetric noise, with early stopping improving performance.
On 15 OpenML binary tabular datasets with 0-30% injected label noise, boosting-based models were the most sensitive to label noise, and random forests were moderately robust.

Among XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost on 15 OpenML-CC18 datasets, no library separated at 10% symmetric noise; separation appeared from 20%, and the ranking depended on both noise rate and noise model.

Significance tests that compare learning algorithms should account for the variability due to the choice of training set, not only that due to test examples; ignoring it can grossly underestimate the variance of the cross-validation estimator. Nadeau and Bengio show that every variance estimator based only on the results of the cross-validation experiment must be biased, and propose new variance estimators whose tests have correct size and good power in simulations.
